doc.title: Vince Lateano interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: State of jazz and aging as a musician
summary: Views on the record industry, rising technical level, and being the elder in a young big band.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well it sure caught my ear, because I was sitting down with this record thinking I wanted to bring a little excerpt here. And that was the one that popped out.
Yeah, record. I notice you said record.
Yeah. Isn’t that something. Well what’s your view on the state of jazz these days? Do you have an opinion on where it’s at?

Well I mean there’s so many things happening in different directions and the record industry is very strange. I mean CDs, the recording industry, it’s almost out of hand it seems like with people — you go to Tower Records which is right here and it’s overwhelming in the product that’s out there. And everybody’s — and this thing about copying and burning CDs, I mean I feel sorry for people that are just trying to get in there. I mean I’m not trying to get — I’m content to be a sideman or just play gigs and just keep playing. As long as I’m playing with good guys it’s fine, I’m happy. I front my own things on occasion. But it’s really spread out now, which is good. I mean I guess it’s healthy that it’s not the same thing, it can’t stay the same way you know. I like playing swinging music and that’s not going to change. But there’s so many influences now that didn’t exist or predominate, the world music influences and the pop and like everything else, a lot of music or a lot of dominant culture music is aimed at a certain age group and you go to a movie and it’s car chases and decapitations. And it’s got to be aimed at somebody. Not me. And I think that music is like that. And the state of jazz, these guys are getting better. I’ll tell you, the level of musicianship, or the level of technicality of people playing an instrument has gone up considerably from when I was starting out. I’ve got kids that are 17 and 18 that I teach in high schools that play a bunch of stuff that I can’t even comprehend practically. And so that part is, and it reflects all the instruments. You hear these kids with saxophones and keyboards and playing all over the instrument. But like everything else with maturity that starts to get better I think. I think that I’m mature so I can appreciate more. But I don’t know I don’t dwell on it, about the old days or this or that, I just keep doing what you’re doing. As long as I’m healthy and doing what I’m doing it’s fine. I play with some younger people. This big band I play with I could, I’m everybody’s father, I could be a grandfather in a couple of instances. I mean I’m going to be 60 next month and there are kids in there that are in their twenties so I guess I could be a grandfather. And I’m playing —
Yeah, all of a sudden you’re the elder statesman.
Yeah they open doors for me.
Yeah. Give me a chair you know.
There could be advantage to that, carrying your drums in and out.
